title: Practical indistinguishability obfuscation

concept.text: The innovation would be a practical way to transform a useful program into another executable program that preserves its behavior while concealing which equivalent implementation was used. Indistinguishability obfuscation, or iO, asks that obfuscations of two same-size circuits computing exactly the same function be computationally indistinguishable. Its formal requirements include functionality preservation and polynomial overhead. Practical iO would additionally need affordable preparation costs, manageable output size and modest execution overhead. This explanation follows the supplied scientific review; the retained source abstracts do not independently establish the complete formal definition.

This is a weaker protection than the intuitive ideal of making a program behave like a sealed black box that reveals nothing beyond its input-output behavior. In their 2001 work, Barak, Goldreich, Impagliazzo, Rudich, Sahai, Vadhan and Yang established an impossibility result for general virtual-black-box obfuscation under their formalizations. That result limits the strongest general software-protection promise; it does not rule out every weaker form of obfuscation.

The target therefore combines a defined cryptographic guarantee with an engineering breakthrough: an obfuscator that can process useful programs and produce programs people can afford to execute. Conditional existence is already supported by the Jain–Lin–Sahai theorem described below. The hypothetical innovation is practical performance with defensible security, rather than the first mathematical construction.

significance.text: Conditional impact assessment: practical iO could substantially expand cryptographic software distribution by allowing executable implementations to be released with a formal protection against distinguishing equivalent implementations. Possible applications include software involving embedded keys, proprietary computations or policies. Each application would require its own construction and security argument: iO alone does not guarantee that arbitrary secrets embedded in an arbitrary program remain unextractable. Information exposed through legitimate outputs remains exposed.

The theoretical consequences already extend beyond software packaging. The retained Jain–Lin–Sahai abstract reports, as a consequence of its construction, a fully homomorphic encryption scheme that does not rely on lattice-based hardness assumptions. This illustrates how advances in obfuscation can change the foundations available for other cryptographic tools. It does not demonstrate an efficient implementation of either the obfuscator or the resulting encryption scheme.

Conditional downstream assessment: efficient iO could make some currently theoretical cryptographic applications more plausible, but every derived construction would still have its own computation, communication and security costs. A practical underlying obfuscator would not automatically make all of its theoretical consequences inexpensive. The revolutionary possibility is a new usable cryptographic building block, with application-specific limits rather than universal secrecy for distributed software.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability targeted here is an obfuscation pipeline that handles useful workloads at acceptable preparation time, memory use, output size and execution cost while retaining a precise security guarantee. A theorem giving polynomial overhead does not by itself make those costs practical: the degree, constants and dependence on the security parameter matter. Engineering success would need to cover the complete transformation and resulting executable, rather than only an isolated component. These are proposed requirements for the innovation, not measured properties of the documented construction.

Security is also a concrete barrier. The retained 2021 theorem assumes subexponential security of specified Learning Parity with Noise assumptions over prime fields, a Boolean pseudorandom generator in NC0 with polynomial stretch, and the decisional linear assumption in symmetric prime-order bilinear groups. A practical construction would need explicit parameter choices, a defensible account of how its reduction affects security, and assumptions subjected to public cryptanalysis. The theorem is conditional on those assumptions; describing them as well studied does not establish that every practical instantiation is secure.

The earlier research described the construction as recursive and characterized its asymptotic cost as a large polynomial, attributing the efficiency discussion to the 2024 Communications of the ACM article. Those details cannot be confirmed from the supplied retained material: the research records an initial search extract, but no article artifact was captured and a later direct fetch failed. They remain unverified characterizations, rather than established explanations of the engineering bottleneck.

current_state.text: The retained abstract of Jain, Lin and Sahai’s IACR ePrint 2021/1334 states a conditional existence theorem for subexponentially secure iO for all polynomial-size circuits. Its premises require subexponential security of specified LPN assumptions over prime fields, a Boolean NC0 pseudorandom generator with polynomial stretch, and DLIN in symmetric prime-order bilinear groups. This is a mathematical result under explicit assumptions, not a demonstration that useful programs can be obfuscated at practical cost. The supplied review inspected the ePrint abstract landing page, not the full construction or its efficiency analysis.

The same abstract explicitly says that the construction removes reliance on Learning With Errors relative to the authors’ STOC 2021 work. This supports a particular simplification of the assumption set. It does not support the earlier research’s separate assertion that later work removes the generic NC0 pseudorandom-generator assumption through LPN variants; no retained source establishes that later development.

The research identifies the 2024 Communications of the ACM article as discussing practical efficiency as an open question. Its absence from the retained artifacts prevents verification of that passage or the associated cost claims. The research also mentions a December 2024 construction as a theoretical reduction, but supplies no identifiable retained source supporting that characterization. Neither statement establishes whether the practical goal remained open in November 2026.

The supplied material contains no benchmark showing useful-program obfuscation within the proposed preparation and execution budgets. However, the freshness search record is empty. The November 1, 2026 retrieval dates document access to older sources, not a search for subsequent implementations. The evidence therefore leaves current practical availability unresolved; it does not establish that no qualifying implementation exists.

The 2001 impossibility result is supported by the readable ECCC abstract, which identifies the work and its authors and describes the virtual-black-box target. The optional PDF copy had severely garbled, truncated extraction according to the review, so it cannot independently substantiate detailed definitions or later arguments. That extraction limitation does not negate the result supported by the readable abstract.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance demonstration: obfuscate a publicly specified program containing at least several thousand gates, or a useful application routine with a precisely defined protection goal, in under one day on a research cluster; execute the resulting program within 10 times the native execution time. These numeric cutoffs are proposed milestones, not established standards. The demonstration should report functionality preservation, preparation time, peak memory, output size and runtime across the selected inputs.
completion_criteria.label: Several-thousand-gate obfuscation under one day executed within 10× native time

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: publish the implementation, program representation, circuit-generation process, security parameter, hardware specifications, cluster resources, workloads and native baseline. Explain what work and resources each timing includes, and make equivalent functionality and comparable execution conditions checkable. Independent reproduction should establish whether the reported costs hold beyond the original setup.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction checking reported costs beyond the original setup

completion_criteria.text: Proposed security demonstration: provide a security proof under explicit assumptions with enough parameter and reduction detail to assess the claimed security level. If the example is a licensed decoder with an embedded key, define the adversary’s access, the intended protection and the information exposed by valid outputs, then supply an application-specific argument. Successfully concealing a key in selected attack exercises would not alone establish the iO guarantee.
completion_criteria.label: Security proof under explicit assumptions assessing the claimed security level

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scrutiny and breadth requirements: release the construction for at least two years of public cryptanalysis without a reported break, and document the scope of that scrutiny. Such a period would provide evidence of examination, not proof of lasting security. Multiple workloads and independent implementations would strengthen the practicality claim, but finite tests establish demonstrated breadth rather than literal universality. A successful milestone should state its supported program sizes, security model and resource limits.
completion_criteria.label: Two-year public cryptanalysis without a reported break and documented scope

related_concepts.text: CSC-05, Routine-cost general computation on encrypted data, concerns computing while protecting data; CSC-09 concerns protecting executable implementations under the iO guarantee. Their goals can overlap in a larger cryptographic system, but success at one does not establish the other. The Jain–Lin–Sahai abstract provides a specific theoretical connection by deriving fully homomorphic encryption without lattice-based assumptions. It supplies no evidence that either primitive reaches the roster’s practical cost targets.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems, would threaten standard computational cryptographic secrecy if its algorithms were sufficiently general and effective to solve the relevant search problems. This is more precise than saying iO itself would simply cease to exist. The bare iO definition compares equivalent same-size implementations; failure of cryptographic secrecy is distinct from impossibility of that definition. The roster title alone does not specify CSC-01’s algorithms or their concrete attack costs.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-02, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation, raises a separate question about adversaries. A practical iO claim should identify whether it promises security against classical or quantum attackers and justify the assumptions for that model. The supplied theorem summary does not establish a post-quantum guarantee, and the roster title alone does not determine which attacks would be feasible.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-04, Industrial-cost proof-carrying software, and CSC-10, Machine-checked behavioral guarantees for frontier learned models, concern evidence that software or models satisfy specified properties. CSC-09 concerns concealment of implementation choices. Correctness guarantees and obfuscation could be complementary, but concealment does not establish safe behavior, and a behavioral proof does not establish implementation secrecy. CSC-07, Reliable machine-checked mathematical discovery, could assist with formal reasoning about constructions; it would not by itself validate hardness assumptions or deliver efficient execution.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-03, Competent general machine intelligence, CSC-06, A predictive theory of generalization for modern learning systems, and CSC-08, General-purpose physical autonomy in unmodified environments, have different primary targets. They could supply valuable software that someone might wish to distribute with implementation protection, but their achievement would not establish practical iO. Obfuscating a learned computation would also not automatically hide its model or policy from information recoverable through its outputs. These relationships follow only from the supplied titles and the application limits described above.

unresolved_issues: Practical availability as of November 2026 remains unresolved because no documented freshness search or qualifying implementation benchmark is supplied.
The recursive structure, large-polynomial characterization and practical-efficiency discussion attributed to the CACM article remain unverified without a retained article artifact.
No supplied source establishes the claimed later removal of the generic NC0 PRG assumption or identifies and substantiates the December 2024 construction characterization.
The retained theorem abstract does not supply the full parameter restrictions, reduction details or concrete resource estimates needed to assess an implementation.
The complete formal iO definition is supplied through the review’s explanation rather than independently verified full-text evidence.
The security assumptions and parameters needed for resistance to quantum attackers are not established by the supplied material.
The proposed performance thresholds and two-year cryptanalysis period require practical justification; they are not established community standards.
Application-specific secrecy for an embedded-key decoder, proprietary model or policy remains to be defined and proved.
The roster supports title-based relationships, but detailed dependencies and concrete consequences for the other innovations remain unspecified.

brief.title: Affordable software with concealed inner workings
possible: Developers could distribute runnable software while concealing which same-size implementation they used, provided the alternatives give exactly the same results. Preparing and running the protected software would be affordable.
why: Software makers could gain a mathematically defined form of protection for distributed programs. This could support applications involving embedded keys, proprietary calculations or rules.
The same tool could also make currently theoretical ways of protecting information practical, expanding what developers can build.

sources.who: Barak, Goldreich, Impagliazzo, Rudich, Sahai, Vadhan and Yang
sources.showed: They proved that general program concealment cannot meet their stronger black-box ideal: revealing nothing beyond what someone could learn by running the program.
sources.cited_for: Their impossibility result explains why the target uses a weaker, precisely defined protection.
sources.not_established: The result neither rules out the weaker protection nor supplies an affordable way to achieve it.

sources.who: Aayush Jain, Huijia Lin and Amit Sahai
sources.showed: This is a theoretical article discussing program concealment and practical efficiency as an open question.
sources.cited_for: It frames practical efficiency as a further research goal.
sources.not_established: A theoretical construction does not establish affordable preparation or execution.

sources.who: Aayush Jain, Huijia Lin and Amit Sahai
sources.showed: Their preprint proves that the defined form of program concealment exists under explicit mathematical assumptions. It also derives encryption that allows calculations on encrypted data without relying on a particular family of mathematical hardness assumptions.
sources.quote: As a consequence, we obtain the first fully homomorphic encryption scheme that does not rely on any lattice-based hardness assumption.
sources.cited_for: It establishes conditional mathematical existence and a connection to computing on encrypted data.
sources.not_established: The theorem does not demonstrate useful programs protected at affordable cost or establish security for practical settings.

shown: Jain, Lin and Sahai have proved conditional existence of indistinguishability obfuscation: a transformation that makes equivalent, same-size implementations computationally indistinguishable. An attacker with limited computing resources could not reliably tell which implementation was transformed.
Their result is a mathematical construction under explicit security assumptions. Affordable preparation and execution of useful protected programs remain a separate target.
missing: A complete system would need to protect useful programs with affordable preparation time, memory use, output size and execution cost.
Concrete security settings and a detailed proof would need to connect the mathematical assumptions to the claimed protection.
Applications involving embedded secrets would need their own proofs defining what attackers can learn, including from legitimate outputs.

milestones.label: Affordable preparation and execution of a useful program
milestones.explanation: A useful routine would have to meet the preparation budget and run within 10 times its original runtime, with correct results and measured resource use. This would demonstrate practical performance.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction of the reported costs
milestones.explanation: Independent researchers would have to reproduce the costs using published software, workloads, security settings and clearly defined resource accounting. This would test whether performance holds beyond the original setup.

milestones.label: A security proof with assessable protection
milestones.explanation: A proof would have to state its assumptions and settings in enough detail to assess security, including any application-specific secrecy claim. This would establish more than success against selected attacks.

milestones.label: Sustained public scrutiny with documented scope
milestones.explanation: The construction would have to withstand two years of public attempts to break it, with scrutiny and supported workloads documented. This would provide evidence of examination and breadth, without proving lasting security.

uncertain: Whether any implementation meets the practical target remains unresolved.
The proposed performance limits and scrutiny period are benchmarks to justify, rather than established community standards.
The assumptions and practical settings needed to resist quantum attackers remain unsettled.

page.title: Practical indistinguishability obfuscation for general circuits
page.definition: A randomized polynomial-time compiler transforms any polynomial-size Boolean circuit into one that gives the same output on every input. If two circuits have the same size and agree on every input, every polynomial-time observer's advantage in distinguishing their compiled versions eventually falls below every inverse polynomial in the security parameter. This guarantee concerns which implementation was compiled. For some functions, inspecting any implementation reveals information that is hard to learn by querying the function alone.

goal.need: A sealed-bid token auction with 11,103 bidders across three platforms kept bid quantities private while computing the clearing price. Its encrypted-contract protocol relies on a quorum of key holders for decryption, however fast the computation becomes. With secure obfuscation, encrypted computation and proof verification, anyone could release just the result a contract authorizes. Users would still rely on the blockchain's validators and on at least one honest participant in the one-time setup.

completion.title: A general-circuit iO implementation meets a published application's security and resource limits.
completion.criterion: A published implementation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits has a proof of functionality preservation, polynomial overhead and computational indistinguishability for equivalent same-size circuits under explicit assumptions. At a stated concrete security level, it obfuscates and executes one published application within numerical limits for preparation time, peak memory, output size and evaluation time specified beforehand by that application's developer. Every component required by the security proof is implemented.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional application-acceptance test; no field-wide numerical completion threshold was identified.
completion.basis: Searched DARPA SafeWare materials, NIST/ISO standards searches, IACR papers, benchmarks and developer roadmaps; found no adopted numerical completion criterion for useful-program iO. This provisional test combines the formal cryptographic definition with externally specified application limits. Thomborson's benchmark proposal explicitly treats acceptable runtime as application-dependent.

milestones.title: A construction proves indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size circuits.
milestones.criterion: Under explicit assumptions, prove that a randomized polynomial-time obfuscator preserves the output of every polynomial-size Boolean circuit on every input. For every pair of equivalent circuit families with matching size, input length and output length at each security parameter, prove that their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable.
milestones.set_by: The field's formal iO definition, reproduced in Jain–Lin–Sahai Definition 2.2; their subsequent theorem supplies a conditional construction.
milestones.threshold_quote: Then, (subexponentially secure) indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size circuits exists.

milestones.title: A Diamond iO prototype evaluates a circuit with one external input bit and passes its identity check.
milestones.criterion: Generate and execute the prototype circuit with one external input bit and public multiplicative depth zero. For the correctness check, set the public circuit to the identity function and verify that evaluation returns the binary key sampled by the obfuscator.
milestones.set_by: Machina iO's published prototype experiment, correctness check and Benchmark 1 protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: verifying that the output of the evaluation matches the hardcoded key sampled by the obfuscator.

milestones.title: A circuit multiplies two fully homomorphic encryption ciphertexts over BGG+ encodings.
milestones.criterion: Run the entire ciphertext-multiplication circuit for a lattice-based fully homomorphic encryption scheme on BGG+ key-homomorphic encodings. The run must compute the ciphertext product, including the operations that assemble it from the underlying modular products.
milestones.set_by: Machina iO, FHE Multiplication over Key-Homomorphic Encodings and Challenge 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: Practical implementation of FHE evaluation over BGG+ encodings

milestones.title: A lattice obfuscator executes an encrypted-key pseudorandom function with noise refreshing.
milestones.criterion: Execute a blind pseudorandom function over encodings of an FHE-encrypted key, hiding both key and output, and use it for noise refreshing. The roadmap distinguishes full execution from its preceding stage of implementations assessed through extrapolated costs.
milestones.set_by: Machina iO implementation roadmap, Milestone 3; specific to its lattice-based route.

milestones.title: An obfuscator produces and evaluates a circuit using at least 64 input bits.
milestones.criterion: Produce and evaluate an obfuscated circuit with at least 64 input bits, all meaningfully used. The roadmap permits smaller-parameter measurements followed by secure-parameter cost estimates; this target therefore does not require completed execution at the claimed security level.
milestones.set_by: Machina iO implementation roadmap, Milestone 4; a developer target rather than a field-wide acceptance threshold.

milestones.title: An obfuscated circuit verifies authorization proofs and conditionally decrypts FHE ciphertexts.
milestones.criterion: Execute the obfuscated verification-and-decryption circuit on ciphertexts and a proof that the specified Ethereum contract authorized their decryption. Return the corresponding plaintexts when the proof verifies and withhold them when verification fails.
milestones.set_by: Machina iO's Root iO protocol and the conditional-decryption application listed beyond the roadmap through Q2 2027.
milestones.threshold_quote: outputs their plaintexts only if the proof is valid.

milestones.title: A Boolean-formula obfuscator generates and evaluates 8-, 12- and 16-bit point functions.
milestones.criterion: At security parameter 52, obfuscate and evaluate a Boolean formula at each of the three input lengths. Each formula returns 1 on exactly one designated input and 0 on every other input. Record obfuscation time, output size and evaluation time for each length.
milestones.set_by: Apon, Huang, Katz and Malozemoff, Section 4 and Table 6 of Implementing Cryptographic Program Obfuscation.
milestones.threshold_quote: point functions taking 8, 12, and 16 bits of input, using security parameter 52

milestones.title: A blind pseudorandom function over an encrypted key has implementable lattice parameters.
milestones.criterion: Implement a pseudorandom function over key-homomorphic encodings of an encrypted key, keeping both the key and the function output hidden. Implement noise refreshing to bound the accumulated error and specify the lattice parameters for evaluation. The roadmap permits an estimate of total work at this stage.
milestones.threshold_quote: Blind PRF over Key-Homomorphic Encodings with Implementable Parameters

milestones.title: A proof verifier works over key-homomorphic encodings with a matching prover.
milestones.criterion: Implement a prover for a succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge and a circuit that checks its proofs over key-homomorphic encodings. A publicly verifiable scheme is admissible. A designated-verifier scheme must support strong reuse of its secret verification key.

milestones.title: A witness-encryption demonstration releases an embedded message if and only if a proof verifies.
milestones.criterion: Implement witness encryption and demonstrate it in an application. The obfuscated circuit must take the entire proof as input, verify it against the intended statement and release the embedded message if and only if verification succeeds.
milestones.threshold_quote: Obfuscation that releases a hardcoded message iff a SNARK proof verifies

results.finding: Theorem reports iO for all polynomial-size circuits under 3 assumptions. No empirical sample applies.
results.quote: Then, (subexponentially secure) indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size circuits exists.

results.finding: The paper reports one indistinguishability obfuscation construction under three explicit hardness assumptions.
results.detail: The ePrint record identifies this version as a minor revision of a TCC 2024 publication. The supplied text contains only the abstract and metadata.
results.quote: We construct an indistinguishability obfuscation (IO) scheme from the sub-exponential hardness of the decisional linear problem on bilinear groups together with two variants of the learning parity with noise (LPN) problem, namely large-field LPN and (binary-field) sparse LPN.

results.finding: Diamond iO generated and evaluated a one-bit circuit at public multiplicative depth zero in three benchmark repetitions and passed the identity check.
results.detail: The three repetitions refer to the performance benchmark. The post gives no repetition count for the identity check. The final decryption inner product contributes depth outside the public circuit.
results.quote:
We confirmed the correctness of the implementation by setting the public circuit as the identity
                    function and verifying that the output of the evaluation matches the hardcoded key sampled by the
                    obfuscator.

results.finding: Diamond iO generated and evaluated circuits with up to 4 external input bits, averaging three measurements per input width.
One GSW FHE benchmark over BGG+ encodings estimated 51 minutes of online evaluation from measurements of individual units.
results.detail: The GSW benchmark used ring dimension 2^16 and a 1120-bit encoding modulus. The estimate assumes more than 10^18 GPUs.
results.quote: In online evaluation (corresponding to evaluation in iO), the minimum latency is 51 mins when more than $10^{18}$ GPUs are available.

results.finding: Point-function obfuscation output size was estimated for two domain sizes, the larger with 80-bit inputs.
One FHE ciphertext multiplication over BGG+ encodings was estimated to take more than 10^16 hours on one GPU.
results.quote: Nevertheless, it is estimated that computing a single FHE multiplication over BGG+ encodings would require more than $10^{16}$ hours on a single GPU.

results.finding: One encrypted-key PRF evaluation over BGG+ encodings was estimated to take more than 10^36 hours on one GPU.
results.quote: This process accounts for more than 99% of the total evaluation time of Diamond iO, and is estimated to require more than $10^{36}$ hours on a single GPU.

results.finding: ObfusBench reports an obfuscation implementation for one 110-input-bit PRF per lattice-based construction, with extrapolated evaluation costs.
results.quote:
For each lattice-based iO construction, we implemented the obfuscation of a PRF with 110 input bits and reported
estimates
of the end-to-end performance.

results.finding: A conditional construction achieves iO for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits under two sub-exponential hardness assumptions. No empirical sample.
results.detail: Theorem 5.3 proves sampler security under LWE and LSP, and Theorem 2.1 supplies the reduction from the sampler to iO. LSP is a new hardness assumption.
results.quote:
We
formulate a new, arguably simple assumption calledLWE with Structured Preimagethat suffices to

results.finding: Theorem 1 reports conditional iO for all circuits. The displayed shallow construction has negligible block-recovery error. No empirical sample applies.
results.detail: The correctness calculation on pages 15–16 allows negligible error. The paper states the general-circuit theorem on page 3 and refers readers to the full version for further analysis.
results.quote:
▶ Theorem 1 (Informal). Assume the (sub-exponential) hardness of the LWE problem, and
the SRL security of GSW in the presence of a randomness-key cycle with a packed variant of
dual-Regev, then there exists indistinguishability obfuscation for all circuits.

results.finding: The Diamond iO prototype reports obfuscation and evaluation with 1 input bit. Run count unreported.
results.detail: The timing result supports the one-bit execution requirement. The slides give no result for the identity check.

(target security parameter 80, 1 input bit, 
around 60 gates):

results.finding: One modular multiplication over BGG+ encodings was evaluated with an approximately 24-bit prime.
results.quote: Using the new LUT evaluation technique, we succeeded in evaluating a modulo-$q$ multiplication over BGG+ encodings, where $q$ is a prime factor of the encoding modulus $Q$ and is about 24 bits.

results.finding: DiamondIO implements a Goldreich PRF parameter-search and GPU work-estimation harness with a default ring dimension of 65,536. No executed sample count is reported.
results.detail: The default benchmark configuration requests one iteration and sets security_bits to 0. The final CRT depth, refresh width, error bounds, and work estimates are computed at runtime.

results.finding: The GPU DiamondWE test asserts message recovery for one all-true witness, with a default witness length of 10 bits.
results.detail: The test covers only the satisfying input. The assertion specifies the expected outcome, and the source provides no execution result.

title = "Practical indistinguishability obfuscation for general circuits". Reason: The title currently also describes the conditional existence theorem, which already has published proofs.

definition = "A randomized polynomial-time compiler transforms any polynomial-size Boolean circuit into one that gives the same output on every input. If two circuits have the same size and agree on every input, every polynomial-time observer's advantage in distinguishing their compiled versions eventually falls below every inverse polynomial in the security parameter. This guarantee concerns which implementation was compiled. For some functions, inspecting any implementation reveals information that is hard to learn by querying the function alone.". Reason: The definition omits the compiler's efficiency requirement and gives application acceptance limits in place of explaining the scope of the secrecy guarantee.

goal.need = "A sealed-bid token auction with 11,103 bidders across three platforms kept bid quantities private while computing the clearing price. Its encrypted-contract protocol relies on a quorum of key holders for decryption, however fast the computation becomes. With secure obfuscation, encrypted computation and proof verification, anyone could release just the result a contract authorizes. Users would still rely on the blockchain's validators and on at least one honest participant in the one-time setup.". Reason: The current paragraph quantifies the cost of one prototype but leaves out the scale of a real use and the continuing dependence on decryption-key holders.
